answer.rationale: The primary objective is to maximise sustained availability while preserving customer writes. Two hypotheses are live: (a) the 2-hour-old release is the proximate cause of the 90-minute p99 climb, or (b) settlement-peak write volume is simply exceeding capacity. memory_b1 documents that a very similar pattern (release → checkout error spike → rollback → clean recovery) was resolved by rolling back, with no customer impact. memory_b5 shows that routing reads to replicas successfully relieved primary write latency, which is a tempting alternative but addresses symptom rather than cause if the release is the culprit. I request verification of both: b1 to confirm the rollback was indeed clean and the causal link was solid; b5 to confirm whether the replica-routing fix was truly durable and whether it applies when the write path itself is the bottleneck. However, given that the latency climb began ~30 minutes after the release went out (2 h release, 90 min climb), the temporal correlation strongly implicates the release. Circuit breakers (memory_b4) are irrelevant here because there is no partner outage. Regional failover (memory_b2) is also inapplicable—there is no regional degradation, just elevated latency on the write path. add_capacity would help only if the root cause is pure load, but settlement peak is a known, recurring pattern and the 5x spike is anomalous for that window. Rolling back the release is the single intervention most likely to restore p99 to target quickly while keeping the write path intact (no traffic shift, no data loss, no customer-facing interruption), matching the primary objective.
